175.title: Foundations and therapeutic communication
175.recall: Compare the patient’s report with what you observe. Match the response to the phase of the therapeutic relationship.

practice.question: A patient says, “My medicine helps the voices, but I feel unsteady when I stand.” What comes first?
choices: Assess standing tolerance, sedation and fall risk.
Advise stopping all medications permanently.
Wait for the next routine visit.
practice.why: The symptom could increase immediate risk of injury. Assess it and communicate findings so the regimen can be reviewed.

practice.question: During the working phase a client avoids group because they expect rejection. What would help?
choices: Decide for the client.
Explore the thought and agree on one manageable action.
Reassure them everyone will like them.
practice.why: Exploring the prediction and trying a small action connects the thought, emotion and behavior.

175.title: Assessment, grief, safety and anxiety
175.recall: Decide whether the patient can process a long explanation right now. Identify the first change that would make the setting unsafe.

practice.question: A patient in a panic is overwhelmed by several people giving advice. Which approach fits?
choices: Hand the patient a long worksheet.
Ask several nurses to question them.
Have one calm nurse stay nearby and use brief directions.
practice.why: Severe anxiety limits attention. A calm presence and simple instructions support orientation while medical causes are assessed.

practice.question: A relative asks for details about a competent adult patient. What should the nurse check first?
choices: What the patient has authorized the team to share.
Which relative called first.
Whether the information would reassure the family.
practice.why: Consent and applicable confidentiality rules guide disclosure.

175.title: Mood, psychosis, eating and substance use
175.recall: Check immediate danger when the stem mentions voices, impulsivity, withdrawal, suicidal thinking or medical instability.

practice.question: A patient says a voice is ordering them to do something frightening. Which question comes first?
choices: How long ago were you diagnosed?
What is the voice saying, and do you feel you might act on it?
Why do you believe it?
practice.why: The content and the patient’s ability to resist guide immediate safety precautions.

practice.question: A patient who has been purging reports palpitations and feels faint. What is the priority?
choices: Start a long discussion about self-image.
Encourage unsupervised exercise.
Assess circulation and obtain prompt evaluation of rhythm and electrolytes.
practice.why: Purging can disturb electrolytes and cardiac conduction.

175.title: Cumulative psychiatric nursing
175.recall: Begin with somatic and neurodevelopmental disorders, disruptive behavior, cognition and psychopharmacology. Then revisit the safety decisions from Exams 1–3.

practice.question: An older patient who usually knows the staff suddenly cannot follow a conversation. Which action fits?
choices: Investigate acute delirium and possible medical causes.
Assume the dementia has progressed.
Defer assessment until tomorrow.
practice.why: The rapid change in attention differs from the patient’s baseline.

practice.question: After starting an antipsychotic, a patient develops high fever, marked stiffness and confusion. What comes first?
choices: Offer reassurance and wait.
Escalate for urgent evaluation of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Schedule a routine review.
practice.why: This cluster can indicate a life-threatening medication reaction.

198.title: Foundations of adult health
198.recall: Connect a change in mentation or breathing to the patient’s baseline, recent medicines and fluid status.

practice.question: A postoperative patient is difficult to awaken and breathing shallowly after an opioid. Which action takes priority?
choices: Offer more analgesia.
Assess and support breathing and call for assistance.
Begin discharge teaching.
practice.why: Increasing sedation with shallow breathing can signal impaired ventilation.

practice.question: An older adult becomes confused over a few hours. Which question best guides your assessment?
choices: How many birthdays have they celebrated?
Have they ever needed glasses?
When were they last at their usual level of attention?
practice.why: Time of onset helps identify an acute change that needs evaluation.

198.title: Respiratory disorders
198.recall: Separate an upper-airway sound from a lower-airway sound and notice when the effort to breathe increases despite less noise.

practice.question: A patient develops new stridor and cannot speak comfortably. Which action has priority?
choices: Activate urgent airway support and assess breathing.
Offer a drink.
Wait for morning rounds.
practice.why: Stridor and difficulty speaking can indicate a threatened upper airway.

practice.question: A patient with severe asthma becomes drowsy and little air movement is audible. Which interpretation fits?
choices: The attack has resolved.
The patient can go home.
Ventilation may be failing and help is needed urgently.
practice.why: Quiet breath sounds with drowsiness can reflect fatigue and dangerously limited airflow.

198.title: Cardiovascular disorders
198.recall: Match the electrical rhythm to perfusion. Distinguish pulmonary congestion, systemic congestion and symptoms suggesting acute coronary syndrome.

practice.question: A patient has new chest pressure, nausea and diaphoresis at rest. What should the nurse do first?
choices: Schedule routine teaching.
Activate the chest-pain response and obtain a prompt ECG.
Encourage a walk to reproduce the pain.
practice.why: Symptoms can reflect acute myocardial ischemia. Prompt assessment and ECG guide further care.

practice.question: Which finding most directly suggests pulmonary congestion?
choices: Crackles with dyspnea when lying flat.
Discoloration over an ankle alone.
An isolated callus.
practice.why: Pulmonary fluid accumulation can cause crackles and orthopnea.

198.title: Renal, urinary and hepatobiliary disorders
198.recall: Follow urine output and perfusion in kidney disease. In cirrhosis, bleeding or a change in mental status can alter the priority immediately.

practice.question: A patient receiving peritoneal dialysis develops abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. What is the priority?
choices: Wait until the next visit.
Encourage strenuous activity.
Promptly report possible peritonitis and follow the sampling protocol.
practice.why: Cloudy effluent with pain needs timely assessment and treatment.

practice.question: A patient with cirrhosis vomits blood and becomes dizzy. What comes first?
choices: Assess airway and circulation and activate urgent help.
Measure abdominal girth before assessing vital signs.
Review a long-term meal plan.
practice.why: Active bleeding may compromise circulation or airway protection.

198.title: Upper and lower GI disorders
198.recall: Use bleeding, perfusion and signs of an acute abdomen to decide which patient you would see first.

practice.question: Which finding during assessment of a patient with peptic ulcer disease needs immediate escalation?
choices: Mild heartburn after a meal.
Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen.
A history of belching.
practice.why: Acute pain with rigidity raises concern for perforation.

practice.question: Which finding suggests that a bowel obstruction may be worsening?
choices: Pain becomes continuous with increasing tenderness.
Distention resolves.
The patient resumes passing gas comfortably.
practice.why: Continuous pain and tenderness raise concern for ischemia or a developing complication.

198.title: Cumulative adult health
198.recall: Start with musculoskeletal trauma, then compare the earliest warnings of deterioration across the five previous exams.

practice.question: After a fracture, pain increases despite prescribed analgesia and passive stretch causes severe pain. The foot has a pulse. What comes first?
choices: Wait for loss of the pulse.
Encourage weight-bearing.
Assess distal neurovascular function and obtain urgent evaluation.
practice.why: Compartment syndrome can occur while distal pulses are still palpable.

practice.question: Which change requires immediate respiratory reassessment?
choices: Stable ankle edema.
New drowsiness and shallow breathing after an opioid.
A chronic dry cough without a change from baseline.
practice.why: An acute change in arousal and ventilation can precede respiratory failure.
